feed.title: LN-GAP : Lightning governed by arbitrary programs

entry.title: LN-GAP : Lightning governed by arbitrary programs
entry.summary:
The recent advancements in blockchain technology have led to innovative methods of resolving disputes within smart contracts, particularly through the use of "venues" as described in a new paper and associated GitHub repository. The paper, which can be accessed [here](https://github.com/AdamISZ/ln-gap/blob/master/docs/paper/lngap-short.pdf), along with its source code available on [GitHub](https://github.com/AdamISZ/ln-gap), introduces a method for playing games like chess and blackjack through Bitcoin's Lightning Network, where disputes are resolved trustlessly.
One of the core challenges addressed by this approach is the inefficiency of handling long-chain games directly on the blockchain due to practicality and scalability issues. Instead, these games can be managed off-chain in channels up to a complexity limit. This limit hinges on the principle that disproving an action (like an illegal move in chess) can be significantly more efficient than proving it, which allows for the resolution of disputes using minimal blockchain space and fewer transactions.
The concept of "venues" plays a pivotal role in this system. A venue essentially acts as an impartial observer that confirms whether actions or moves in a game were made correctly and on time. Unlike traditional proof mechanisms which require a unique history, a venue simply verifies if a particular message was published before a set deadline. This setup helps prevent equivocation, where a participant might make conflicting claims to different parties.
However, the system can still be vulnerable to collusion between a venue operator and a player. For instance, if a venue operator colludes with one player to delay confirming a move, it could unfairly disadvantage the opposing player. Despite this potential flaw, the design ensures that the venue never holds any funds, thus eliminating certain types of financial attacks and reducing risks associated with contract manipulation.
In terms of wider applications beyond gaming, this dispute resolution mechanism can be adapted for services such as decentralized storage proofs, similar to those used in Filecoin but with enhanced mechanisms for adjudicating non-compliance. This could involve imposing penalties for service failures, thereby offering a sort of insurance against loss of data.
The paper also explores the feasibility of applying this dispute resolution framework to arbitrary programs of any complexity, despite the inherent limitations of Bitcoin’s scripting language. This is achieved by off-chain bisection of disputes, maintaining a constant on-chain footprint regardless of program complexity.
Overall, the development of this technology reflects a significant step forward in using blockchain for complex contract disputes without compromising on scalability and efficiency. It opens up possibilities for broader applications in various decentralized systems, potentially transforming how contractual disputes are managed in a blockchain environment.
